final_answer:
SHORT ANSWER. Yes. The first and most urgent step is a motion to reopen and rescind the August 1, 2025 in absentia removal order, filed with the immigration court (EOIR) under INA 240(b)(5)(C)(ii) (8 U.S.C. 1229a(b)(5)(C)(ii)) on the ground of lack of notice. That ground has no deadline, and the motion carries no filing fee. The I-130/I-485 denials must then be attacked separately, and the best route runs through the reopened court case and USCIS.

1. Immigration court: motion to reopen and rescind (file now).
An in absentia order may be rescinded at any time if the respondent shows he did not receive notice under INA 239(a)(1) or (a)(2). That is the lack-of-notice ground, and it carries an automatic stay of removal while the motion is pending. INA 239(a)(1) requires the NTA to be given in person or, if personal service is not practicable, by mail to the alien or his counsel of record. INA 239(a)(2) governs notices of hearing. Under Campos-Chaves v. Garland, 602 U.S. 447 (2024), rescission requires showing that notice failed under both (a)(1) and (a)(2) for the hearing that was missed. Here the NTA was reportedly mailed only to an address the couple never gave, and the facts suggest no hearing notice reached him. So the argument is that he never received any statutory notice, and the order should be rescinded. The facts to prove are that the address was never provided by him, that he never received the NTA or hearing notice, that he never received the RFE, that he acted promptly on learning of the order on April 1, 2026, and that he has a basis for relief.
Statutory notice by mail is also tied to the address the alien provides. INA 239(a)(1)(F) requires him to give an address, and written notice goes to the last address provided. A mailing to an address he never provided is not notice he can be charged with. Courts also presume mailing is regular, so he should file a sworn declaration plus his I-485 and I-130 receipts and forms showing the correct address. Do not rely on the exceptional-circumstances ground, which has a 180-day limit that has already run (August 1, 2025 to about January 28, 2026).
If the NTA was never properly served, the court may also be asked to terminate or to hold that jurisdiction never vested, but the primary request should be rescission and reopening.
What to file: a written motion with a cover page, filed through the EOIR Courts and Appeals System (ECAS) or on paper with the immigration court that issued the order, served on DHS/ICE OPLA. Include a sworn declaration, exhibits, and a proposed order. Also file Form EOIR-33/IC (change of address), and Form EOIR-28 if he has counsel. Ask for an automatic stay and, if needed, an emergency stay. If a final order exists and removal is feared, also request a stay of removal from the court.
Fees: none for a motion under INA 240(b)(5)(C)(ii) (lack of notice). The exemption is in 8 CFR 1003.24(b)(2) and EOIR's fee rules, and the 2025 One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA) EOIR fee schedule exempts this motion. The ordinary motion-to-reopen fee does not apply. By contrast, an exceptional-circumstances motion would carry fees. EOIR figures are about $145 plus the OBBBA motion-to-reopen fee of about $920 for FY2026, rising to about $1,095 total on Oct. 1, 2026. These are secondary-source figures I could not confirm on the primary government pages. If the motion were instead a fee-bearing one, a fee waiver (Form EOIR-26A) would be available only for the base fee, not the OBBBA fee.
If the motion is granted, the court will reset the hearing, the NTA is served properly, and the proceedings reopen. Before then, no fee. After reopening, any new application for relief (e.g., adjustment) filed with the court has its own fee: the I-485 filing fee is paid to USCIS or the court per the instructions, and the biometric services fee may apply.

2. Contesting the I-130 denial (USCIS).
The I-130 was denied for abandonment (failure to respond to the RFE). Under 8 CFR 103.2(b)(15), a denial for abandonment cannot be appealed to the BIA or AAO, but a motion to reopen under 8 CFR 103.5 may be filed (Form I-290B). The motion must show the decision was in error because, among other grounds, the request for evidence was sent to an incorrect address. That ground applies here. The usual 30-day deadline (33 if mailed) has long passed (denial was December 5, 2023), so the motion would need USCIS to excuse the late filing under 103.5(a)(1)(i), which allows it only if the delay was reasonable and beyond the petitioner's control. USCIS handling of the RFE mailed to a wrong address is strong support, but USCIS discretion is real. Pair this with a request for the I-130 file and a FOIA request for the record to show what address USCIS used. Alternatively, file a new I-130 (new fee, about $675 paper or $625 online, to confirm) and rely on the marriage. A denial for abandonment does not bar refiling, 8 CFR 103.2(b)(15). A new I-130 is the practical backstop, since the wife is a U.S. citizen and the husband is an immediate relative with no visa-number wait.

3. Contesting the I-485 denial.
The I-485 denial itself (January 15, 2024) was a consequence of the I-130 denial and cannot be administratively appealed. 8 CFR 103.3 and 1245.2 govern. The better path is that once proceedings are reopened, the immigration judge has jurisdiction to adjudicate adjustment of status de novo, 8 CFR 1245.2(a)(1) and (a)(5)(ii), so the denial is renewed rather than overturned. The adjustment would require an approved or approvable I-130 (the IJ cannot approve the I-130, so DHS/USCIS must adjudicate it, and the court may continue the case). As the spouse of a U.S. citizen who was inspected and admitted on a B-2, he is generally eligible under INA 245(a) and exempt from the 245(c) bars as an immediate relative. A USCIS motion on the I-485 denial is also possible but is not the best route, and an I-485 is typically not reopenable by the IJ without the underlying petition.

4. Risks and issues to prepare for.
A. Preconceived intent and misrepresentation. He married 19 days after entering on a B-2. Under the State Department 30/60-day guidance (9 FAM 302.9-4), a marriage within 30 days of entry can support a presumption of willful misrepresentation under INA 212(a)(6)(C)(i). A waiver under 212(i) requires hardship to the USC spouse. This should be addressed in the evidence. The I-130 RFE may have concerned bona fides, so the bona fide marriage evidence must be strong.
B. Overstay and the in absentia order. If the order is not rescinded, the order of removal remains enforceable and a 10-year bar (INA 212(a)(9)(A)) may apply upon departure. The in absentia order also bars most discretionary relief for 10 years (INA 240(b)(7)), but this is lifted if the order is rescinded. An immediate-relative adjustment applicant is not subject to the 245(c) overstay bar.
C. Federal court. If the motion is denied, he can petition the circuit court of appeals for review within 30 days of the BIA decision (appeal to the BIA is due within 30 days of the IJ denial), and the Supreme Court in Campos-Chaves and Niz-Chavez v. Garland, 593 U.S. 155 (2021), set the notice requirements.
D. Compliance with Matter of Lozada (8 I&N Dec. 637) is not needed unless an ineffective assistance claim is raised.

PRACTICAL SEQUENCE: (1) Immediately file a motion to reopen with EOIR for lack of notice, no fee, with a stay request. (2) In parallel, prepare I-290B for the I-130 or a new I-130. (3) After reopening, renew the I-485 before the IJ and ask for continuances pending I-130 adjudication. Consult an immigration attorney, since some details (current fee amounts, Chief IJ filing instructions, circuit law) vary and I could not verify the primary-source text of 8 CFR 1003.23 and 1003.24 within this run.

authorities.title: Rescission of in absentia order
authorities.proposition: In absentia order may be rescinded at any time if alien did not receive notice under 239(a)(1) or (2); filing the motion stays removal.

authorities.title: Campos-Chaves v. Garland
authorities.proposition: Rescission for lack of notice requires showing no notice under either 239(a)(1) or (a)(2) for the missed hearing.

authorities.title: Denial for abandonment
authorities.proposition: Abandonment denial cannot be appealed but may be the subject of a 103.5 motion, including where request was sent to an incorrect address; does not preclude refiling.

authorities.title: EOIR fees for motions
authorities.proposition: No fee for motion to reopen in absentia order under INA 240(b)(5)(C)(ii).

authorities.title: Inflation Adjustment for EOIR OBBBA Fees; Fiscal Year 2026
authorities.proposition: OBBBA motion-to-reopen fee adjusted for inflation; in absentia lack-of-notice motion exempt (per search summary only).

authorities.title: Reopening or reconsideration (USCIS)
authorities.proposition: 30-day deadline for USCIS motions; late filing excused only if reasonable and beyond control.

claims.text: A lack-of-notice motion to reopen an in absentia order can be filed at any time with the immigration court and stays removal.
No EOIR filing fee applies to a motion under INA 240(b)(5)(C)(ii).
The abandonment-based I-130 denial cannot be appealed but can be challenged by a 103.5 motion (I-290B) on the incorrect-address ground, or by refiling.
Rescission requires showing no notice under both 239(a)(1) and (a)(2).
